passage:
Tuesday (Sarita wrote the date for me on top)

I am writing so I don't lose today.
This morning I stood in the kitchen and could not remember why. The kettle was in my hand. I felt my chest go tight, like falling in a dream. I shouted at nobody. Then I sat down and cried, which I do not like to do.
Sarita, my granddaughter, came in. She did not rush me. She said, "Dadu, shall we make tea together?" and I remembered, yes, tea.
I know something is wrong with my head. I cannot say what. It makes me angry and ashamed.
But she held my hand while the water boiled and asked about my village. I told her about the mango tree. I remembered all of it.

Sumit

qa.q: What was in Sumit's hand in the kitchen?
qa.a: The kettle was in his hand.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when he could not remember why he was in the kitchen?
qa.a: He felt frightened, with his chest tight like falling in a dream, and later angry and ashamed.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that helped Sumit keep his dignity?
qa.a: She didn't rush him, gently suggested making tea together, held his hand and asked about his village.

qa.q: What might Sarita feel as she helps her Dadu?
qa.a: She probably feels tender and patient, wanting him to feel safe and still himself.

grounding: It shows a person with memory loss feeling frightened, angry and ashamed, knowing something is wrong, while still feeling love and needing dignity.

passage:
Anjali Nani: Aadhya where am I
Anjali Nani: at a shop. forgot the way home
Aadhya: Nani, I'm here. Stay inside the shop, okay? Can you see a name on the board?
Anjali Nani: Gupta Medical. near a temple
Aadhya: Good. That's two streets from your house. Mamu is coming to get you. I've called him.
Anjali Nani: I feel so foolish. I have walked here fifty years
Aadhya: You're not foolish. Your memory is playing tricks, that's all. It's not your fault.
Anjali Nani: don't tell everyone
Aadhya: I'll only tell Mamu and Mummy, so we can keep you safe. Can you ask the shopkeeper for a chair?
Anjali Nani: yes. he gave me water
Aadhya: I love you, Nani.
Anjali Nani: I love you. my Aadhya
Anjali Nani: Mamu is here

qa.q: What was the name on the shop's board?
qa.a: The board said Gupta Medical, near a temple.

qa.q: How did Nani feel about getting lost?
qa.a: She felt frightened and foolish, embarrassed because she had walked there for fifty years.

qa.q: Which of Aadhya's replies helped keep Nani safe and respected?
qa.a: Asking her to stay in the shop, sending Mamu, telling her it wasn't her fault, and sharing only with those who could help.

qa.q: What was this chat like for Aadhya?
qa.a: It was probably frightening for Aadhya, who still stayed calm so Nani would feel safe and loved.

grounding: It shows a person with memory loss who is lost and embarrassed but still loving, and a grandchild treating her with dignity while getting her home safely.

passage:
'Dadu, it's Tanuja. Your granddaughter.'
Arnab looked at her face for a long moment. 'I know. I know that.' His hands twisted the edge of his shawl. 'I just… I lost the word.'
'It's okay.'
'It isn't okay.' His voice rose. 'I went to the kitchen three times today and forgot why. Your Dida's photo is on the wall and I couldn't remember her name. Do you know how that feels?'
Tanuja sat beside him. 'It sounds frightening.'
'It is.' His anger crumbled. 'And I'm embarrassed. I used to teach mathematics. Now I can't find the bathroom.'
'You're still my Dadu. You taught me my tables.'
He smiled faintly. 'Seven sevens?'
'Forty-nine.'
'Good girl.' He patted her hand. 'At least I haven't forgotten that.'

qa.q: What subject did Arnab use to teach?
qa.a: Mathematics.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling as he talked about forgetting?
qa.a: He felt frightened, angry and embarrassed, aware that something was wrong with his memory.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that kept Arnab's dignity?
qa.a: She listened, named his fear, reminded him who he still was and joined him in the times-tables game.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt hearing Dadu forget Dida's name?
qa.a: She was probably sad and shaken, but chose to stay calm and warm for him.

grounding: Shows a person living with memory loss feeling frightened, angry and embarrassed yet still loving, and a granddaughter treating him as a whole person.

passage: My name is Gurpreet, and I know something is wrong with me. Last month I got lost driving to my own daughter Charu's house, a route I've driven a hundred times. I sat in the car outside a strange temple and cried, and I haven't cried since my wife died. Charu calls me Papa and hugs me, but sometimes I can see the worry in her eyes when I ask the same thing twice. The doctor has a word for it now. I don't like the word. I hate the way people start speaking slowly to me, as if I'm a child. I still love my granddaughter's drawings. I still feel embarrassed when I spill my tea. I'm still me in here, even when I can't find the door. I just want them to remember that.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet get lost driving to?
qa.a: Charu's house.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet feel when people speak slowly to him?
qa.a: He feels hurt and belittled, as if being treated like a child.

qa.q: What would help Gurpreet feel respected?
qa.a: Being spoken to normally and treated as the same person, with feelings and dignity, even when he forgets.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Gurpreet asks the same thing twice?
qa.a: She probably feels worried and sad, seeing her father change.

grounding: Shows a person living with memory loss who is frightened and aware something is wrong, yet still feels love, embarrassment and dignity and wants to be treated as himself.

passage:
Day centre note, Thursday
Nirmala, who lives with dementia, arrived upset this morning. She kept asking where her handbag was and accused another member of taking it. When I tried to guide her to a chair, she pushed my hand away and shouted, 'Don't treat me like a baby!' I stepped back and spoke to her as I would any adult. 'You're right, I'm sorry. Let's look for it together.' We found it under her chair. She looked embarrassed. 'I'm getting so stupid.' I told her she wasn't stupid, and that losing things is part of the illness, not her fault. Later she showed me a photo of her granddaughter on her phone and glowed as she told me about her. She laughed at the singing session. Please let her family know she had a good afternoon.
Avni, day centre carer

qa.q: Where did Avni and Nirmala find the handbag?
qa.a: Under her chair.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she said she was getting stupid?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed after accusing someone and finding the bag herself.

qa.q: What did Avni do that protected Nirmala's dignity?
qa.a: Avni apologised, spoke to her as an adult, searched with her and reassured her it was the illness, not her fault.

qa.q: How might the member Nirmala accused have felt?
qa.a: That person may have felt hurt or shocked at being accused, even if they understood it was the illness.

grounding: Shows a person with dementia feeling frightened, angry and embarrassed yet still loving and proud, and a carer treating her with dignity as a person.

passage:
Tuesday. Tushar wrote the date at the top for me. He says writing helps.
This morning I stood in the kitchen holding a spoon and could not remember why. My own kitchen. I felt the floor tilt. When Tushar came in, I pretended I was checking the spoon for rust. He didn't laugh. He said, "Tea?" and I said yes, and the day came back a little.
In the afternoon I called the neighbour by my sister's name. I saw her face and wanted to hide under the bed like a child. I got angry at Tushar for no reason, then sorry.
But tonight he played the old shabads on the radio and I sang every word. Every word. He held my hand. I know this boy. I love this boy.
Baljeet

qa.q: Who wrote the date at the top of the page?
qa.a: Tushar wrote the date at the top.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel after calling the neighbour by the wrong name?
qa.a: Baljeet felt deeply embarrassed, wanting to hide under the bed, and then turned angry and sorry.

qa.q: What did Tushar's responses get right?
qa.a: He didn't correct or laugh, offered tea to steady the moment, and used music Baljeet loved, treating Baljeet as a whole person.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tushar when Baljeet gets angry for no reason?
qa.a: It probably hurts Tushar a little, but he stays gentle, and the singing at night shows the love is still shared.

grounding: Illustrates a person living with memory loss feeling frightened, embarrassed and angry, yet still feeling love and dignity and needing to be treated as a person.
